Covariance-Aware Transformers for Quadratic Programming and Decision Making

Kutay Tire ††thanks: Equal contribution. Affiliation: The University of Texas at Austin Email: kutaytire@utexas.edu    Yufan Zhang Email: yufanzh@umich.edu    Ege Onur Taga Affiliation: University of Michigan Email: egetaga@umich.edu    Samet Oymak Affiliation: University of Michigan Email: oymak@umich.edu
Abstract

We explore the use of transformers for solving quadratic programs and how this capability benefits decision-making problems that involve covariance matrices. We first show that the linear attention mechanism can provably solve unconstrained QPs by tokenizing the matrix variables (e.g. AA of the objective 12​x⊤​A​x+b⊤​x\frac{1}{2}x^{\top}Ax+b^{\top}x) row-by-row and emulating gradient descent iterations. Furthermore, by incorporating MLPs, a transformer block can solve (i) ℓ1\ell_{1}-penalized QPs by emulating iterative soft-thresholding and (ii) ℓ1\ell_{1}-constrained QPs when equipped with an additional feedback loop. Our theory motivates us to introduce Time2Decide: a generic method that enhances a time series foundation model (TSFM) by explicitly feeding the covariance matrix between the variates. We empirically find that Time2Decide uniformly outperforms the base TSFM model for the classical portfolio optimization problem that admits an ℓ1\ell_{1}-constrained QP formulation. Remarkably, Time2Decide also outperforms the classical “Predict-then-Optimize (PtO)” procedure, where we first forecast the returns and then explicitly solve a constrained QP, in suitable settings. Our results demonstrate that transformers benefit from explicit use of second-order statistics, and this can enable them to effectively solve complex decision-making problems, like portfolio construction, in one forward pass.

1 Introduction

Quadratic programming (QP) is a central tool in modern optimization, underlying applications in control, machine learning, and finance. Its canonical form is

minx⁡12​x⊤​A​x+b⊤​xsubject toC​x⪯d,\min_{x}\;\frac{1}{2}x^{\top}Ax+b^{\top}x\quad\text{subject to}\quad Cx\preceq d,

where A,bA,b define the objective and C​x⪯dCx\preceq d encodes constraints. Beyond this template, many practically important variants, including ℓ1\ell_{1}-regularized and ℓ1\ell_{1}-constrained formulations, remain convex and capture structural requirements such as sparsity, budgets, and transaction-cost constraints.

We study the following concrete question: To what extent can transformer architectures act as general-purpose QP solvers, and how does this capability translate into improved decision making when second-order statistics (e.g., covariance matrices) matter? This focus is motivated by two observations: First, there is growing evidence that transformers can emulate iterative algorithms and optimization procedures through their attention-and-residual structure (e.g., theories of in-context learning showing gradient-descent-like behavior). Second, many high-stakes decision problems are naturally expressed as QPs whose inputs include covariances. However, standard transformer pipelines, specifically time-series foundation models, do not explicitly incorporate such second-order information, even when it is essential for the downstream task.

A standard example is portfolio optimization. Classical mean–variance allocation solves a QP whose parameters depend on forecasted returns and an (estimated) covariance matrix. A fundamental and widely used baseline is the two-stage (or predict-then-optimize) pipeline: first predict the unknown parameters (e.g., returns), then solve the resulting QP with a conventional optimizer (Markowitz, 1952; Elmachtoub and Grigas, 2022, e.g.,). While well established, this decoupling can be statistically suboptimal: when forecasts are noisy, the plug-in solution can overreact and yield inferior decisions. Indeed, one can formalize an explicit scenario where the predict-then-optimize (PtO) rule is strictly dominated by a Bayes-optimal end-to-end policy that shrinks noisy estimates before optimizing (Prop. 5.1).

As our central contribution, we develop a comprehensive theory on how and when transformers can solve regularized QPs. Our constructions are highly compute-efficient and capture the individual contributions of the attention mechanism, MLP, and looping. Building on this theory, we introduce Time2Decide, a generic method to endow time-series foundation models (TSFMs) with transformer-based optimization that is covariance-aware. Concretely, Time2Decide augments the TSFM input with tokens that explicitly represent the covariance structure, enabling the model to learn an end-to-end mapping from historical context to decisions in one forward pass. The overview of our setup is provided in Figure 1. This directly targets the limitation highlighted above: by training to predict the eventual decision variable, the model can learn the proper amount of attenuation/calibration in the presence of estimation noise, rather than committing to a brittle plug-in rule. Empirically, Time2Decide consistently improves over (i) the base TSFM and (ii) supervised fine-tuning of the TSFM without covariance information, and it can even outperform the classical two-stage PtO procedure that forecasts returns and then solves the QP explicitly. In particular, while PtO is highly competitive, Time2Decide surpasses it in regimes where end-to-end calibration matters most, aligning with the strict separation exhibited by Proposition 5.1 and illustrating how explicitly admitting second-order statistics can enable transformers to solve two-step decision problems within a single learned model. Our contributions are:

  • •

    Quadratic programming theory. We provide explicit constructions showing how transformer components can emulate classical first-order methods for multiple QP classes, including unconstrained, linearly constrained, ℓ1\ell_{1}-regularized, and ℓ1\ell_{1}-constrained programs.

  • •

    Experimental validation. We demonstrate that transformers can indeed learn the mapping from tokenized QP instances to optimal solutions, with linear attention variants offering strong empirical performance.

  • •

    Our Method: Time2Decide. We integrate QP-solving capabilities into TSFMs via covariance-augmented tokenization, enabling end-to-end forecasting and decision-making. Focusing on portfolio optimization, our proposed method Time2Decide outperforms fine-tuning a TSFM thanks to its special covariance tokens. Importantly, it also outperforms the two-stage Predict-then-Optimize (PtO) baseline under realistic scenarios. Specifically, when (i) the returns are not too predictable or (ii) the portfolio transition constraints are not too tight. We complement these through theoretical insights (Proposition 5.1) where end-to-end decision-making can provably and strictly dominate two-stage optimization.

Together, our results position transformers as both (i) theoretically grounded algorithm emulators for regularized QPs and (ii) practical end-to-end decision makers when second-order/covariance information is essential.

2 Related Work

Theoretical Analysis of In-Context Learning

Recent work has developed theoretical frameworks for understanding in-context learning in transformers. Akyürek et al. (2023), Von Oswald et al. (2023) and Dai et al. (2023) demonstrated that transformers emulate gradient descent during ICL. Xie et al. (2022) offered a Bayesian perspective, while Zhang et al. (2023); Zhang et al. (2024) showed transformers learn linear models in-context. Ahn et al. (2023) established that they implement preconditioned gradient descent, and Mahankali et al. (2024) proved that one-step gradient descent is optimal for single-layer linear attention. Multiple works (Li et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024; Bai et al., 2023; Gozeten et al., 2025; Shen et al., 2024) studied the generalization capability of transformers. However, these works largely focus on fully-supervised settings where the in-context examples are input–label pairs for regression or classification. In contrast, our theoretical results show that the same attention-and-residual structure can emulate first-order optimization methods when the in-context tokens encode problem data rather than labeled examples.

Neural Networks as Optimizers.

In recent research, neural networks have been harnessed as optimizers in several directions. Villarrubia et al. (2018) showed that multilayer perceptrons can approximate non‑linear objective functions and transform them into polynomial forms so that classical methods apply when Lagrange multipliers are impractical. Differentiable layers such as Amos and Kolter (2017) treat a quadratic program as a network module, derive gradients via implicit differentiation, and use a custom interior‑point solver, while Magoon et al. (2024) decouple gradient computation from the choice of QP solver by exploiting the active set of constraints. In Nair et al. (2020), neural heuristics improve mixed‑integer solvers by learning variable assignments and branching policies. Chen and Liu (2022) treat the objective itself as a neural network and optimize it via backpropagation, handling multi‑objective cases with little sensitivity to variable dimension. Chen et al. (2022) showed that graph neural networks can predict feasibility, boundedness, and approximate solutions for linear programs. Our study differs by feeding quadratic programs directly into transformers and proving that with appropriate tokenization, these sequence models can emulate iterative solvers while handling linear and ℓ1\ell_{1} constraints. Beyond demonstrating feasibility, we provide a systematic analysis of how transformer attention mechanisms capture the structure of quadratic programs, and we show empirically that our model achieves competitive accuracy. In this way, our work establishes transformers themselves as standalone, general-purpose optimizers for constrained quadratic programs.

Multivariate Time-Series Transformers.

Early neural approaches to multivariate forecasting relied on encoder–decoder RNNs and temporal convolutional networks; however, their receptive fields or recurrence limited long-range context. Transformer variants now dominate the landscape. Temporal Fusion Transformer (TFT) augments attention mechanism with gating and interpretable variable selection (Lim et al., 2021). Informer introduces ProbSparse self-attention for efficient long-sequence inference (Zhou et al., 2021), while Autoformer and FEDformer decompose series into trend and seasonal tokens to improve long-horizon extrapolation (Wu et al., 2021; Zhou et al., 2022). Crossformer (Zhang and Yan, 2023) and Spacetimeformer (Grigsby et al., 2021) rearrange inputs to model cross-dimension dependencies explicitly, and PatchTST (Nie et al., 2023) treats fixed-length segments as tokens to boost locality. Most recently, TimePFN uses permutation-equivariant networks pre-trained on synthetic data to provide strong zero-shot generalization (Taga et al., 2025). These advances demonstrate the transformer’s flexibility in processing diverse token structures and incorporating auxiliary information, setting the foundation for integrating optimization-solving capabilities alongside forecasting tasks in multivariate time-series models.

3 Theoretical Results

3.1 Problem Setup

Notation.

Let [p]={1,…,p}[p]=\{1,\dots,p\} for an integer p≥1p\geq 1. Lowercase letters (e.g., x,yx,y) denote vectors; uppercase letters (e.g., A,CA,C) denote matrices. For A∈ℝn×nA\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}, let λmax​(A)\lambda_{\max}(A) be its largest eigenvalue and ‖A‖2\|A\|_{2} its operator norm. We write ⟨u,v⟩=u⊤​v\langle u,v\rangle=u^{\top}v, use ∥⋅∥2\|\cdot\|_{2} for the Euclidean norm, and ∥⋅∥1\|\cdot\|_{1} for the ℓ1\ell_{1} norm. For u∈ℝu\in\mathbb{R}, set [u]+=max⁡{u,0}[u]_{+}=\max\{u,0\} (applied elementwise to vectors). The soft-thresholding map is 𝒮θ​(y)=sign⁡(y)⊙(|y|−θ)+\mathcal{S}_{\theta}(y)=\operatorname{sign}(y)\odot(|y|-\theta)_{+}, and Proj{∥⋅∥1≤B}\operatorname{Proj}_{\{\|\cdot\|_{1}\leq B\}} denotes Euclidean projection onto the ℓ1\ell_{1}-ball. We use proxψ⁡(y)=arg⁡minx​{12​‖x−y‖22+ψ⁡(x)}\operatorname{prox}_{\psi}(y)=\arg\min_{x}\{\tfrac{1}{2}\|x-y\|_{2}^{2}+\psi(x)\} and write L=λmax​(A)L=\lambda_{\max}(A).

Quadratic programs.

We study four convex QPs, each specified by problem data and a stepsize pair (γ,η)(\gamma,\eta):

(U) minx∈ℝn⁡12​x⊤​A​x+b⊤​x,\displaystyle\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}}\ \tfrac{1}{2}\,x^{\top}Ax+b^{\top}x, (1)
(LC) minx∈ℝn⁡12​x⊤​A​x+b⊤​xs.t.C​x⪯d,\displaystyle\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}}\ \tfrac{1}{2}\,x^{\top}Ax+b^{\top}x\ \ \text{s.t.}\ \ Cx\preceq d, (2)
(R) minx∈ℝn⁡12​x⊤​A​x+b⊤​x+λ​‖x‖1,λ>0,\displaystyle\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}}\ \tfrac{1}{2}\,x^{\top}Ax+b^{\top}x+\lambda\|x\|_{1},\qquad\lambda>0, (3)
(C) minx∈ℝn⁡12​x⊤​A​x+b⊤​xs.t.‖x‖1≤B,B>0.\displaystyle\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}}\ \tfrac{1}{2}\,x^{\top}Ax+b^{\top}x\ \ \text{s.t.}\ \ \|x\|_{1}\leq B,\quad B>0. (4)

Throughout, we assume A≻0A\succ 0; for (LC) we also assume the feasible set {x:C​x⪯d}\{x:\,Cx\preceq d\} is nonempty.

Algorithms to be emulated.

Let xkx_{k} (and, when present, λk⪰0\lambda_{k}\succeq 0) denote the current iterate(s), and write L=λmax​(A)L=\lambda_{\max}(A). We have the following algorithms:

GD (U)

Unconstrained Gradient Descent:

xk+1=xk−γ⁡(A​xk+b),0<γ<2L.x_{k+1}=x_{k}-\gamma(Ax_{k}+b),\qquad 0<\gamma<\frac{2}{L}. (5)
Arrow–Hurwicz (LC)

For problems with linear constraints:

xk+1=xk−γ⁡(A​xk+b+C⊤​λk),λk+1=[λk+η⁡(C​xk+1−d)]+,0<γ<2L,η​γ​‖C‖22<1.\begin{aligned} x_{k+1}&=x_{k}-\gamma(Ax_{k}+b+C^{\top}\lambda_{k}),\\ \lambda_{k+1}&=\big[\lambda_{k}+\eta(Cx_{k+1}-d)\big]_{+},\end{aligned}\qquad\begin{gathered}0<\gamma<\frac{2}{L},\\ \eta\gamma\|C\|_{2}^{2}<1.\end{gathered} (6)
ISTA (R)

Iterative Shrinkage-Thresholding Algorithm for regularization:

yk=xk−γ⁡(A​xk+b),xk+1=𝒮γ​λ(yk)=proxγλ∥⋅∥1(yk),0<γ≤1L.\begin{aligned} y_{k}&=x_{k}-\gamma(Ax_{k}+b),\\ x_{k+1}&=\mathcal{S}_{\gamma\lambda}(y_{k})=\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma\lambda\|\cdot\|_{1}}(y_{k}),\end{aligned}\qquad 0<\gamma\leq\frac{1}{L}. (7)
PGD with ℓ1\ell_{1}-projection (C)

Projected Gradient Descent onto the ℓ1\ell_{1}-ball:

yk=xk−γ⁡(A​xk+b),xk+1=Proj{∥x∥1≤B}(yk),0<γ≤1L.\begin{aligned} y_{k}&=x_{k}-\gamma(Ax_{k}+b),\\ x_{k+1}&=\operatorname{Proj}_{\{\|x\|_{1}\leq B\}}(y_{k}),\end{aligned}\qquad 0<\gamma\leq\frac{1}{L}. (8)

We present explicit weight constructions showing how small transformer fragments implement one iteration of classical first-order methods for QPs. Tokens encode the current iterate xkx_{k}, the multiplier λk\lambda_{k} when needed, and rows of problem data (e.g., AA, CC). A residual on the xx-row propagates the iterate, and repeating these one-step maps yields the standard convergence behavior under the usual step size conditions of the target algorithms. The summary of the required architectures for each algorithm is presented in Table 1.

3.2 Unconstrained QP via Single-Block Linear Attention

We show that a single linear-attention head with a residual connection simulates one step of gradient descent for the unconstrained QP defined in Section 3.1.

Proposition 3.1.

A single linear-attention head that attends from the xx-row to the AA-rows, followed by a residual on the xx-row, realizes the update xk+1=xk−γ⁡(A​xk+b)x_{k+1}=x_{k}-\gamma(Ax_{k}+b). Hence, for any 0<γ<2/L0<\gamma<2/L, the iterates converge linearly to x⋆=−A−1​bx^{\star}=-A^{-1}b.

Construction.

We store tokens for the rows of AA, the vector bb, and the current iterate xkx_{k}, and we design fixed query, key, and value maps WQ,WK,WVW_{Q},W_{K},W_{V} (see Appendix A.1). Then the resulting q,k,vq,k,v yield, when evaluated at the xx-token is o=A​xk+bo=Ax_{k}+b. Applying a residual with post-map −γ​I-\gamma I on the xx-row yields

xk+1=xk−γ​o=xk−γ⁡(A​xk+b).x_{k+1}=x_{k}-\gamma\,o=x_{k}-\gamma(Ax_{k}+b).

Full token layout and selector matrices are given in the Appendix A.1. Furthermore, we empirically validate this construction in Figure 2(a) and discuss the algorithmic complexity in Appendix B.1. ∎

3.3 Linearly Constrained QP via Single Macro-Block Linear Attention

We now turn to the linearly constrained QP, the second formulation presented in Section 3.1.

Proposition 3.2.

A single macro-block consisting of two self-attention blocks and a residual on the xx-row realizes the sequential update

xk+1=xk−γ⁡(A​xk+b+C⊤​λk),\displaystyle x_{k+1}=x_{k}-\gamma\big(Ax_{k}+b+C^{\top}\lambda_{k}\big), (9)
λk+1=[λk+η⁡(C​xk+1−d)]+.\displaystyle\lambda_{k+1}=\big[\lambda_{k}+\eta\,(Cx_{k+1}-d)\big]_{+}. (10)

Let L=λmax​(A)L=\lambda_{\max}(A) and let ∥⋅∥2\|\cdot\|_{2} denote the operator norm. If the feasible set {x:C​x⪯d}\{x:\,Cx\preceq d\} is nonempty and the step sizes satisfy 0<γ<2/L0<\gamma<2/L and η​γ​‖C‖22<1\eta\gamma\|C\|_{2}^{2}<1, then the iterates (xk,λk)(x_{k},\lambda_{k}) converge to a KKT point.

Construction.

We fix WQ,WK,WVW_{Q},W_{K},W_{V} so that two heads in the first linear-attention block, evaluated at the xx- and λ\lambda-tokens, produce

oA​x+b=A​xk+b,oC⊤​λ=C⊤​λk,o^{Ax{+}b}=Ax_{k}+b,\qquad o^{C^{\top}\lambda}=C^{\top}\lambda_{k},

which yields the primal update

xk+1=xk−γ⁡(oA​x+b+oC⊤​λ)=xk−γ⁡(A​xk+b+C⊤​λk).x_{k+1}=x_{k}-\gamma\big(o^{Ax{+}b}+o^{C^{\top}\lambda}\big)=x_{k}-\gamma\big(Ax_{k}+b+C^{\top}\lambda_{k}\big).

We then run a second attention block with a single head evaluated at xk+1x_{k+1}, obtaining

oC​x−d=C​xk+1−d,o^{Cx{-}d}=Cx_{k+1}-d,

and apply a token-wise ReLU for the dual step,

λk+1=[λk+η​oC​x−d]+.\lambda_{k+1}=\big[\lambda_{k}+\eta\,o^{Cx{-}d}\big]_{+}.

Full WQ,WK,WVW_{Q},W_{K},W_{V} specifications and calculations of the linear attention blocks appear in Appendix A.2, together with the per-iteration cost analysis in Appendix B.2. ∎

3.4 Sparse QPs via Single-Block Linear Attention: ℓ1\ell_{1}-Regularized and ℓ1\ell_{1}-Constrained

We now introduce sparsity via an ℓ1\ell_{1} penalty (R) or an ℓ1\ell_{1} budget (C)—corresponding to the last two QP formulations in Section 3.1—and extend the (U) block, without changing the attention mechanism, to realize proximal and projected gradient descent algorithms.

Proposition 3.3.

One (U) gradient step followed by a fixed two-layer ReLU FFN with a scalar threshold θ=γ​λ\theta=\gamma\lambda yields

xk+1=𝒮θ(xk−γ(Axk+b))=proxγλ∥⋅∥1(yk).x_{k+1}=\mathcal{S}_{\theta}\!\big(x_{k}-\gamma(Ax_{k}+b)\big)=\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma\lambda\|\cdot\|_{1}}(y_{k}).

With 0<γ≤1/L0<\gamma\leq 1/L, the objective F⁡(x)=12​x⊤​A​x+b⊤​x+λ​‖x‖1F(x)=\tfrac{1}{2}x^{\top}Ax+b^{\top}x+\lambda\|x\|_{1} decreases and xkx_{k} converges to a minimizer.

Construction.

We compute yk=xk−γ⁡(A​xk+b)y_{k}=x_{k}-\gamma(Ax_{k}+b) with the (U) head and implement soft-thresholding with a fixed two-layer width-2​n2n ReLU FFN with weights

since (u−θ)+−(−u−θ)+=sign⁡(u)​(|u|−θ)+(u-\theta)_{+}-(-u-\theta)_{+}=\mathrm{sign}(u)\,(|u|-\theta)_{+} coordinatewise. With θ=γ​λ\theta=\gamma\lambda, this equals proxγλ∥⋅∥1(yk)\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma\lambda\|\cdot\|_{1}}(y_{k}), i.e., the ISTA update. Full steps are provided in Appendix A.3. Figure 2(b) shows that the transformer construction matches ISTA’s convergence behavior across depth. ∎

Proposition 3.4.

One (U) gradient step followed by the same fixed two-layer ReLU FFN wrapped in a scalar threshold loop performs the exact Euclidean projection onto the ℓ1\ell_{1}-ball:

xk+1=Proj{∥x∥1≤B}(xk−γ(Axk+b)).x_{k+1}=\mathrm{Proj}_{\{\|x\|_{1}\leq B\}}\!\big(x_{k}-\gamma(Ax_{k}+b)\big).

4 Neural QP Solver Experiments

Our theoretical findings demonstrate that a transformer architecture has the expressive power to represent the computational steps of various QP-solving algorithms. In this section, we move from theoretical possibility to empirical validation. We conduct a series of experiments to determine if a transformer can learn the complex mapping from a QP’s parameters to its optimal solution through data-driven training alone, without being explicitly programmed with an iterative algorithm. 11 1 Our main code is available on https://github.com/mziycfh/QP_transformer.

4.1 Experimental Design

We conduct a controlled function-approximation study to assess whether transformer architectures can generalize across families of linearly-constrained QPs. The task is to learn a mapping from a tokenized QP instance to its optimal solution. Each instance is of the form:

minx∈ℝn⁡12​x⊤​A​x+b⊤​xs.t.C​x⪯d,\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}}\ \tfrac{1}{2}\,x^{\top}Ax+b^{\top}x\quad\text{s.t.}\quad Cx\preceq d,

where the dataset generator samples the problem data (A≻0A\succ 0, bb, CC, and dd) and computes the ground-truth optimal solution x⋆x^{\star} for supervision.

Our default configuration uses n=5n{=}5 variables and m=3m{=}3 constraints with datasets of 50k/10k/10k train/validation/test instances. Problem coefficients are sampled as: (i) AA is constructed as A=G​G⊤+0.1​IA=GG^{\top}+0.1I where G∼𝒩⁡(0,I)G\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I) to ensure it is positive definite; (ii) b∼𝒩⁡(0,I)b\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I); (iii) C∼𝒩⁡(0,I)C\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I); and (iv) d∼Uniform​(1,2)d\sim\text{Uniform}(1,2).

To prepare the data for the models, we tokenize each QP instance into a sequence of length n+m+3n+m+3. This sequence consists of one token for each row of A∈ℝn×nA\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} and C∈ℝm×nC\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} (total n+mn+m tokens), plus three additional tokens for the vector bb, a zero-padded version of dd, and a random initializer xinitx_{\mathrm{init}}. Each token is a vector in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}. More details can be found in Appendix C.1.

Model architectures and metrics.

We compare two encoder-only transformer variants: a SoftmaxTransformer and a LinearTransformer. The SoftmaxTransformer employs standard multi-head self-attention with softmax normalization, computing attention weights as softmax​(Q​KT/dk)\text{softmax}(QK^{T}/\sqrt{d_{k}}). In contrast, the LinearTransformer uses a more efficient linear attention mechanism that replaces the softmax operation with element-wise products. For a comparison against parameter-matched non-attention baselines (MLP, LSTM) on the same QP tokenization, see Appendix D.

To evaluate these architectures, we perform a hyperparameter sweep over model depth (number of layers) and the number of attention heads. Performance is primarily assessed using the coefficient of determination (R2R^{2}) and Normalized Mean Squared Error (NMSE) on the solution vector, with Mean Squared Error (MSE) as the training loss. The metrics are defined as:

MSE=1n∥x^−x⋆∥22,NMSE=‖x^−x⋆‖22‖x⋆‖22,R2=1−‖x^−x⋆‖22‖x¯⋆−x⋆‖22,\begin{gathered}\text{MSE}=\tfrac{1}{n}\|\hat{x}-x^{\star}\|_{2}^{2},\quad\text{NMSE}=\tfrac{\|\hat{x}-x^{\star}\|_{2}^{2}}{\|x^{\star}\|_{2}^{2}},\\[6.0pt] R^{2}=1-\tfrac{\|\hat{x}-x^{\star}\|_{2}^{2}}{\|\bar{x}^{\star}-x^{\star}\|_{2}^{2}},\end{gathered} (11)

where x^\hat{x} is the predicted solution, x⋆x^{\star} is the ground-truth optimal solution, and x¯⋆\bar{x}^{\star} is the mean of all ground-truth solutions in the test set. In addition, we report downstream feasibility via constraint violation and optimality via objective sub-optimality in Appendix E. We report n=5,m=3n=5,m=3 in the main text and defer other settings to the supplementary materials.

4.2 Experimental Results

Function-approximation accuracy.

Our experimental results demonstrate that transformers are capable of learning to solve QP problems. The best-performing LinearTransformer (8 layers, 2 heads) and SoftmaxTransformer achieved an R2R^{2} of 0.974 and 0.935, respectively. Notably, there is a performance advantage for the LinearTransformer architecture. As summarized in Table 2, the LinearTransformer consistently outperforms the SoftmaxTransformer across the hyperparameter grid. This finding suggests that linear attention mechanisms are particularly well-suited for the numerical reasoning required in QP function approximation. The superior accuracy of the LinearTransformer is further detailed in Figure 3, which shows the tight distribution of its Normalized Mean Squared Error (NMSE) on the test set. Additional neural QP solver results for higher-dimensional settings are provided in Appendix E.

Robustness to distribution shift.

To investigate the robustness of our models, we conduct experiments where the training and test distributions differ in the condition number of the QP problems. The condition number, κ⁡(A)=λmax​(A)/λmin​(A)\kappa(A)=\lambda_{\max}(A)/\lambda_{\min}(A), controls the numerical difficulty of the optimization, with higher values corresponding to more ill-conditioned problems that are harder to solve. We generate this distribution shift by controlling the eigenvalue spread of the AA matrix using a scaling parameter κ\kappa, which creates exponentially more difficult problems for higher κ\kappa values. To isolate this effect, we normalize the Frobenius norm of AA to match the baseline distribution.

The results of this analysis are shown in Table 3. We trained the best-performing models (LinearTransformer with 8 layers/2 heads and SoftmaxTransformer with 16 layers/2 heads) on the baseline distribution and tested them on shifted distributions with varying κ\kappa ranges. Both architectures demonstrate considerable robustness, indicating they can generalize reasonably well to more challenging numerical conditions. Again, the LinearTransformer consistently shows superior performance and a more graceful degradation across all κ\kappa ranges as the problem difficulty increases.

The strong performance and robustness of our transformer-based QP solvers motivate their integration into foundation models for sequential decision-making. We demonstrate that QP solving can be seamlessly incorporated through supervised fine-tuning by simply adding relevant tokens to the input sequence. The following section showcases this integration through a portfolio optimization case study, where we embed QP solving within a time series foundation model to enable end-to-end decision-making under complex structural constraints.

5 Decision Making with Covariance-Aware Transformers

In many high-stakes domains like finance and operations, downstream decision rules are solved via quadratic programs with structural constraints. A natural approach is to first forecast the relevant parameters and then solve the QP explicitly—the predict-then-optimize (PtO) pipeline. However, this two-stage approach can be suboptimal as noisy forecasts can lead to overly aggressive decisions.

Proposition 5.1 (Informal: PtO is suboptimal under estimation noise).

In a two-asset mean–variance problem with a Gaussian prior on the mean gap and noisy observations, the PtO plug-in rule is strictly dominated in expected utility by the Bayes-optimal policy, which shrinks the estimate by a factor ρ<1\rho<1 before optimizing.

While the optimal shrinkage depends on unknown noise parameters, an end-to-end model can learn analogous attenuation directly from the decision loss. Providing covariance information helps the model calibrate how aggressively to react to forecast signals. We formalize this result in Appendix F.

We validate this insight through a portfolio optimization case study, where allocations must satisfy non-negativity, budget, and ℓ1\ell_{1} rebalancing constraints. This setting highlights a practical way to integrate second-order information into foundation-model backbones for decision-making in an end-to-end fashion.

5.1 Problem Formulation and Data

We consider a portfolio optimization problem with mm assets over TT time periods. At time tt, we observe the vector of asset returns 𝐫t∈ℝm\mathbf{r}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{m} (where rt,ir_{t,i} represents the return of asset ii at time tt) and must choose portfolio weights 𝐬t∈ℝm\mathbf{s}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{m} (where st,is_{t,i} represents the fraction of wealth allocated to asset ii at time tt) subject to the constraints:

𝐬t\displaystyle\mathbf{s}_{t} ⪰𝟎\displaystyle\succeq\mathbf{0} (no short selling for simplicity),\displaystyle\text{(no short selling for simplicity)}, (12)
𝟏⊤​𝐬t\displaystyle\mathbf{1}^{\top}\mathbf{s}_{t} =1\displaystyle=1 (allocation weights sum to 1),\displaystyle\text{(allocation weights sum to 1)},
‖𝐬t−𝐬t−1‖1\displaystyle\|\mathbf{s}_{t}-\mathbf{s}_{t-1}\|_{1} ≤γ\displaystyle\leq\gamma (transaction cost limit).\displaystyle\text{(transaction cost limit)}.

The rebalancing constraint ‖𝐬t−𝐬t−1‖1≤γ\|\mathbf{s}_{t}-\mathbf{s}_{t-1}\|_{1}\leq\gamma restricts the total absolute change in portfolio weights, where γ\gamma represents the maximum allowed rebalancing budget. This constraint proxies transaction costs and prevents excessive portfolio turnover.

To establish a target for supervised training, we compute an oracle allocation, 𝐬t⋆\mathbf{s}_{t}^{\star}. This oracle represents the ideal decision at each step, calculated by solving a mean-variance optimization problem assuming perfect foresight of the next period’s returns, 𝐫t\mathbf{r}_{t}. The objective is to maximize risk-adjusted returns:

𝐬t⋆=arg⁡max𝐬t​𝐬t⊤​𝐫t−λ​𝐬t⊤​𝚺^t​𝐬ts.t. ​(12)​ holds. \mathbf{s}_{t}^{\star}=\arg\max_{\mathbf{s}_{t}}\ \mathbf{s}_{t}^{\top}\mathbf{r}_{t}-\lambda\,\mathbf{s}_{t}^{\top}\hat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{t}\mathbf{s}_{t}\quad\text{s.t. }(\ref{eq:portfolio_constraints})\text{ holds. }

Here, 𝚺^t\hat{\bm{\Sigma}}_{t} is the empirical covariance matrix estimated from historical returns, and λ=0.1\lambda=0.1 is the risk aversion parameter that balances expected return against portfolio variance. The oracle solution 𝐬t⋆\mathbf{s}_{t}^{\star} represents the optimal allocation given perfect knowledge of future returns 𝐫t\mathbf{r}_{t}.

Data generation.

We synthesize multivariate time series using the Linear Model of Coregionalization (LMC) as described in Journel and Huijbregts (2003), 𝐗i​(t)=∑j=1rwi​j​fj​(t)\mathbf{X}_{i}(t)=\sum_{j=1}^{r}w_{ij}f_{j}(t), where fj​(t)f_{j}(t) are latent Gaussian processes with varied kernels, wi​jw_{ij} are mixing weights, and rr sets the covariance rank. We then process these time series by scaling with ϵ=0.01\epsilon=0.01 and clipping to the range [−0.3,0.8][-0.3,0.8] to simulate asset returns. We generate separate training and evaluation datasets: 300 training series and 30 evaluation series, each with m=16m=16 assets and T=1024T=1024 time steps. After obtaining the series of returns, we finalize the input sequences by concatenating historical returns and allocations (a total of 2​m2m channels), enabling the model to reason jointly over past market dynamics and portfolio positions. We use sequence length L=96L=96, forecast horizon H=96H=96, and a stride of 1 for training data augmentation.

5.2 Experimental Setup

Proposed architecture.

There exist many transformer-based multivariate time series models. Among them, TimePFN—adapted from one of the strongest baselines, PatchTST (Nie et al., 2023)—serves as the backbone of our approach. Time2Decide augments TimePFN with Covariance-Augmented Tokenization (CAT): it computes the empirical covariance matrix over the normalized input window of 96 previous steps, maps each covariance row to a token via a multi-layer nonlinear projection, prepends the resulting mm covariance tokens to the standard patch embeddings, applies a unified positional encoding to the entire sequence, and processes them jointly through self-attention. After encoding, we remove the covariance tokens and pass only the temporal tokens to the output projectors to generate predictions for both returns and allocations.

Baselines.

We evaluate our proposed model, Time2Decide, against a suite of baselines: (i) Oracle (perfect-foresight allocation, the upper bound in performance for any strategy); (ii) Predict-then-Optimize (TimePFN-predicted returns are fed into a conventional mathematical QP solver to compute allocations under the constraints); (iii) Pretrained (TimePFN used purely as a neural forecaster without covariance tokens); (iv) SFT (supervised fine-tuned TimePFN variant); (v) Uniform (equal-weight allocation).

Training and Inference.

SFT and Time2Decide are trained with a combined loss that balances return and allocation prediction:

ℒ=λr​‖𝐫^−𝐫‖22+‖𝐬^−𝐬⋆‖22,\mathcal{L}=\lambda_{r}\|\hat{\mathbf{r}}-\mathbf{r}\|_{2}^{2}+\|\hat{\mathbf{s}}-\mathbf{s}^{\star}\|_{2}^{2},

where λr\lambda_{r} is a weighting hyperparameter. We find the optimal λr\lambda_{r} for each model via a hyperparameter sweep.

In inference, to ensure all portfolio constraints are satisfied, the model’s raw output 𝐬^\hat{\mathbf{s}} is projected into the feasible set by solving the following QP:

𝐬t=arg⁡min𝐱⁡‖𝐱−𝐬^‖22,s.t. ​𝐱⪰0, 1⊤​𝐱=1,‖𝐱−𝐬t−1‖1≤γ\begin{gathered}\mathbf{s}_{t}=\arg\min_{\mathbf{x}}\|\mathbf{x}-\hat{\mathbf{s}}\|_{2}^{2},\\ \text{s.t. }\mathbf{x}\succeq 0,\ \mathbf{1}^{\top}\mathbf{x}=1,\ \|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{s}_{t-1}\|_{1}\leq\gamma\end{gathered} (13)
Evaluation.

We use a training set of 300 multivariate return series and an evaluation set of 30 series. All experiments use a risk coefficient of λ=0.1\lambda=0.1. We evaluate each strategy across a range of rebalancing budgets γ∈{0.5,0.75,1.0,1.25,1.5,1.75,2.0}\gamma\in\{0.5,0.75,1.0,1.25,1.5,1.75,2.0\}. Performance is measured by the Mean Squared Error (MSE) between the model’s predicted allocations and the oracle’s allocations. Crucially, the MSE is computed on the raw model predictions before the feasibility projection, providing a stringent standard for evaluation. More experimental details can be found in Appendix C.2.

5.3 Experimental Results

Table 4 summarizes the MSE of each strategy across rebalancing budgets γ\gamma. We report the best MSE for each learning-based method after selecting the optimal combined-loss weights λr\lambda_{r} from our sweep, and provide additional results and hyperparameter details in Appendix H. Overall, Time2Decide consistently improves over SFT-TimePFN and Pretrained-TimePFN, highlighting the benefit of incorporating covariance information and learning decisions end-to-end. Predict-then-Optimize (PtO), which relies on exact conventional solvers, achieves the lowest errors at small rebalancing budgets (e.g., 0.02450.0245 at γ=0.5\gamma=0.5 and 0.02940.0294 at γ=0.75\gamma=0.75).

A natural interpretation is that for small γ\gamma, the turnover constraint tightens the feasible set and effectively clips how much the portfolio can change from one step to the next; in this conservative regime, even imperfect return estimates translate to limited action variation, making the plug-in PtO baseline particularly strong. On the other hand, as γ\gamma increases, the feasible set loosens, leaving more room for estimation noise to induce larger portfolio changes, so calibration becomes more important. This aligns with the mechanism highlighted in Appendix F: when decisions are sensitive to noisy inputs, an optimal policy benefits from attenuating overconfident reactions, whereas a plug-in rule corresponds to a fixed, no-attenuation response. Consistent with this view, Time2Decide shows superior performance at larger budgets, surpassing PtO and achieving the best results at higher γ\gamma values (e.g., 0.04420.0442 at γ=1.75\gamma=1.75 and 0.04880.0488 at γ=2.0\gamma=2.0).

Under Noise.

We additionally evaluate performance in a noisy-environment setting. Concretely, we inject Gaussian noise into the return series (scaling by 0.010.01, adding 𝒩⁡(0,0.01)\mathcal{N}(0,0.01), and clipping), and then recompute all downstream quantities using the corrupted data. This includes re-estimating any covariance inputs and recomputing the oracle allocations from the noisy returns. We then report MSE between each strategy’s allocations and the corresponding noisy-data oracle. As shown in Table 5, Time2Decide dominates most strategies across budgets, while PtO degrades as γ\gamma increases. This confirms that end-to-end learning effectively mitigates input noise, aligning with the theory in Appendix F.

6 Conclusion

In this paper, we presented a theoretical and empirical study of how transformer architectures can be explicitly constructed to solve classes of quadratic programs. By carefully designing attention heads and feed-forward modules, we showed that single transformer blocks can emulate gradient descent, primal–dual iterations, and proximal updates for unconstrained, linearly constrained, and sparse QPs. These constructions demonstrate that transformers can effectively replicate the iterative structures of classical optimization algorithms.

On the experimental side, we verified that transformers can learn to solve QPs when trained on tokenized problem instances, with linear attention variants consistently achieving higher accuracy. Extending beyond the original task, we showed that incorporating covariance information as tokens enables end-to-end decision making under structural constraints. Our results highlight that embedding second-order problem data into the transformer input leads to meaningful improvements over baselines. Overall, our results connect classical optimization methods with transformers, showing that transformers can efficiently emulate iterative solvers. Future directions include extending to broader optimization tasks, integrating with other foundation models or reinforcement learning for decision making, and studying the theoretical boundaries of such algorithmic emulation.

Construction.

We add a dual token λk∈ℝ≥0m\lambda_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{m}_{\geq 0}. As in the unconstrained case, we split tokens into content and ID parts and embed every token to a common width p:=2​n+mp:=2n+m (zero-padded), then append a constant slot to reach p′:=p+1p^{\prime}:=p+1. Let

Appendix B Computational Cost per Iteration

Our constructions implement one solver iteration per transformer layer. Therefore, it is natural to compare the cost of a single transformer step to the corresponding first-order iteration. We organize our analysis by problem class: unconstrained and ℓ1\ell_{1}-penalized QPs (Subsection B.1), which depend only on the variable dimension nn, and linearly constrained QPs (Subsection B.2), which depend on both nn and the number of constraints mm. We report the multiplicative overhead:

Overhead=TransformerClassical.\text{Overhead}\;=\;\frac{\text{Transformer}}{\text{Classical}}\,.

B.1 Per-Iteration Cost for (U), (R), and (C)

These three problem classes—corresponding to Propositions 3.1, 3.3, and 3.4—involve only the quadratic matrix A∈ℝn×nA\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} and vectors in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}, with no explicit linear inequality constraints. The computational cost depends solely on the variable dimension nn.

Asymptotic complexity.

For dense QPs, both classical GD/ISTA and our transformer steps are dominated by the matrix–vector product A​xAx, which costs O⁡(n2)O(n^{2}) time per iteration. ISTA additionally applies soft-thresholding at O⁡(n)O(n) cost, negligible relative to n2n^{2} in the dense regime. For ℓ1\ell_{1}-constrained PGD, the classical exact projection onto the ℓ1\ell_{1}-ball runs in O⁡(n​log⁡n)O(n\log n) time, whereas our threshold-loop projection costs O⁡(T​n)O(Tn) for TT inner updates; the overall step remains dominated by the O⁡(n2)O(n^{2}) product.

Wall-clock time per step.

Table 6 reports per-step timing for these three problem classes.

Discussion.

For Gradient Descent and ISTA, the transformer step achieves near iteration-level parity with overheads of 1.041.04–1.35×1.35\times across dimensions. Projected Gradient Descent exhibits larger overhead at small nn due to the O⁡(T​n)O(Tn) threshold-loop projection, but this decreases from 3.37×3.37\times at n=16n{=}16 to 1.14×1.14\times at n=128n{=}128 as the O⁡(n2)O(n^{2}) matrix–vector product dominates.

B.2 Per-Iteration Cost for (LC)

The linearly constrained problem class—corresponding to Proposition 3.2—involves explicit linear inequality constraints C​x⪯dCx\preceq d with constraint matrix C∈ℝm×nC\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}. The Arrow–Hurwicz primal-dual method requires two sequential attention blocks per iteration: one for the primal update and one for the dual update. The computational cost depends on both the variable dimension nn and the number of constraints mm.

Asymptotic complexity.

Each Arrow–Hurwicz iteration requires forming A​xAx at O⁡(n2)O(n^{2}) cost, plus C​xCx and C⊤​λC^{\top}\lambda at O⁡(m​n)O(mn) cost each, giving O⁡(n2+m​n)O(n^{2}+mn) per step. The ReLU operation for dual feasibility adds O⁡(m)O(m) cost, which is negligible.

Wall-clock time per step.

Table 7 reports per-step timing for various (n,m)(n,m) configurations.

Discussion.

The Arrow–Hurwicz transformer construction achieves overheads ranging from 0.99×0.99\times to 1.25×1.25\times across all tested configurations. Notably, at (n,m)=(64,32)(n,m)=(64,32), the transformer construction is faster than the classical implementation, likely due to improved memory access patterns from the unified token representation Z=[Q;C;c;d;x;λ]Z=[Q;C;c;d;x;\lambda]. As problem size increases, overheads remain modest (1.191.19–1.20×1.20\times at n=128n{=}128), demonstrating that the two-block attention structure required for primal-dual updates does not introduce significant computational burden beyond the single-block constructions.

Appendix C Experimental Details

In this section, we provide comprehensive details regarding the setup of our experiments to ensure reproducibility. All experiments are implemented in PyTorch and executed on NVIDIA L40S GPUs.

C.1 Neural QP Solver

C.1.1 QP Dataset Generation

We generate synthetic QP instances of the form minx⁡12​x⊤​A​x+b⊤​x​ s.t. ​C​x⪯d\min_{x}\frac{1}{2}x^{\top}Ax+b^{\top}x\text{ s.t. }Cx\preceq d. The symmetric positive definite matrix A∈ℝn×nA\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} is constructed as A=G​G⊤+0.1​IA=GG^{\top}+0.1I, where entries of G∈ℝn×nG\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}, as well as b∈ℝnb\in\mathbb{R}^{n} and constraint matrix C∈ℝm×nC\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}, are sampled from a standard normal distribution 𝒩⁡(0,1)\mathcal{N}(0,1). The bound vector d∈ℝmd\in\mathbb{R}^{m} is sampled from the uniform distribution 𝒰⁡[1,2]\mathcal{U}[1,2]. Ground truth solutions x∗x^{*} are computed using the OSQP solver accessed via CVXPY. For problem dimension configurations (n,m)∈{(5,3),(7,3),(7,6),(10,3),(10,6),(10,9)}(n,m)\in\{(5,3),(7,3),(7,6),(10,3),(10,6),(10,9)\}, we generate a dataset consisting of 50,00050,000 training samples, 10,00010,000 validation samples, and 10,00010,000 test samples. For larger instances with configurations (n,m)∈{(15,10),(20,8),(20,16)}(n,m)\in\{(15,10),(20,8),(20,16)\}, we increase the dataset size to 100,000100,000 training samples, 20,00020,000 validation samples, and 20,00020,000 test samples to ensure sufficient coverage of the higher-dimensional space.

C.1.2 Model Architectures

We evaluate two architectures: SoftmaxTransformer, which uses standard scaled dot-product attention, and LinearTransformer, which employs the linear attention mechanism. Both models project the input problem data (tokenized rows of A,CA,C and vectors b,db,d) into a hidden embedding dimension of dmodel=256d_{\text{model}}=256. We conduct a grid search over model depth L∈{1,2,4,8,16,32}L\in\{1,2,4,8,16,32\} and the number of attention heads H∈{1,2,4,8}H\in\{1,2,4,8\} to analyze the impact of model capacity. A dropout rate of 0.10.1 is applied during training to prevent overfitting.

C.1.3 Training

All models are trained to minimize the Mean Squared Error (MSE) between the predicted xx and the ground truth optimal solution x∗x^{*}. We use the AdamW optimizer with an initial learning rate of 1×10−41\times 10^{-4} and a weight decay of 0.020.02. We utilize a learning rate scheduler (ReduceLROnPlateau) that reduces the learning rate by a factor of 0.50.5 if the validation loss does not improve for 55 epochs, with a minimum learning rate of 10−610^{-6}. The random seed is fixed at 4242 for all experiments to ensure reproducibility. Training proceeds for a maximum of 500500 epochs. To prevent overfitting, we employ early stopping with a patience of 3030 epochs, monitoring the validation loss.

C.2 Decision Making with Covariance-Aware Transformers

C.2.1 Data Generation

We utilize LMC to generate synthetic financial return data with dynamic covariance structures. The generative process uses the following specific hyperparameters to simulate market conditions: dirichlet_min=0.01, dirichlet_max=0.75, weibull_shape=6, and weibull_scale=125. Each generated time series has a length of T=1024T=1024. For our experiments, we construct training datasets of size Ntrain=300N_{\text{train}}=300 and evaluation datasets of size Neval=30N_{\text{eval}}=30. The input sequence length (lookback window) LL is set to 96.

C.2.2 Inference

During inference, we utilize a rolling window protocol across all strategies. At each time step tt, the system accesses a historical context window to update the portfolio. The specific mechanism for computing the next allocation 𝐬t\mathbf{s}_{t} depends on the strategy:

  • •

    (i) Oracle: At time tt, it uses the ground-truth return 𝐫t\mathbf{r}_{t} (perfect foresight) and the empirical covariance matrix 𝚺^t\hat{\mathbf{\Sigma}}_{t} estimated from the previous L=96L=96 returns. It solves the constrained QP problem using the OSQP solver via the CVXPY interface:

    max𝐬t\displaystyle\max_{\mathbf{s}_{t}}\quad 𝐬t⊤​𝐫t−λ​𝐬t⊤​𝚺^t​𝐬t\displaystyle\mathbf{s}_{t}^{\top}\mathbf{r}_{t}-\lambda\mathbf{s}_{t}^{\top}\hat{\mathbf{\Sigma}}_{t}\mathbf{s}_{t}
    s.t. 𝐬t∈Δm,‖𝐬t−𝐬t−1‖1≤γ\displaystyle\mathbf{s}_{t}\in\Delta_{m},\quad\|\mathbf{s}_{t}-\mathbf{s}_{t-1}\|_{1}\leq\gamma

    where Δm\Delta_{m} is the standard simplex. The resulting 𝐬t\mathbf{s}_{t} is utilized for the next step’s turnover constraint.

  • •

    (ii) Uniform: A naive baseline where the portfolio is equally distributed across all assets at every step, i.e., 𝐬t,i=1m\mathbf{s}_{t,i}=\frac{1}{m}.

  • •

    (iii) Predict-then-Optimize: First, a pretrained TimePFN model uses the history of actual returns 𝐫t−L:t−1\mathbf{r}_{t-L:t-1} to forecast the expected return vector 𝐫^t\hat{\mathbf{r}}_{t}. The empirical covariance matrix 𝚺^t\hat{\mathbf{\Sigma}}_{t} is estimated from the actual history 𝐫t−L:t−1\mathbf{r}_{t-L:t-1}. We then solve the same QP problem as the Oracle, but using the predicted return 𝐫^t\hat{\mathbf{r}}_{t} instead of the ground truth.

  • •

    (iv) End-to-End Neural Strategies (Time2Decide, Pretrained, SFT): These models generate allocations directly without solving a QP explicitly. At time tt, the input window HtH_{t} consists of past actual returns 𝐫t−L:t−1\mathbf{r}_{t-L:t-1} and past projected allocations 𝐬t−L:t−1\mathbf{s}_{t-L:t-1}. The models output a raw prediction vector 𝐬~t\tilde{\mathbf{s}}_{t}. To ensure validity, we apply a differentiable projection layer that maps 𝐬~t\tilde{\mathbf{s}}_{t} to the closest valid allocation 𝐬^t\hat{\mathbf{s}}_{t} satisfying the simplex and turnover constraints:

    min𝐬^t\displaystyle\min_{\hat{\mathbf{s}}_{t}}\quad ‖𝐬^t−𝐬~t‖22\displaystyle\|\hat{\mathbf{s}}_{t}-\tilde{\mathbf{s}}_{t}\|_{2}^{2}
    s.t. 𝐬^t∈Δm,‖𝐬^t−𝐬t−1‖1≤γ\displaystyle\hat{\mathbf{s}}_{t}\in\Delta_{m},\quad\|\hat{\mathbf{s}}_{t}-\mathbf{s}_{t-1}\|_{1}\leq\gamma

    This projection is solved using an SLSQP solver. The window for the next time step t+1t+1 is updated autoregressively: we discard the oldest observation and append the actual realized return 𝐫t\mathbf{r}_{t} and the valid projected allocation 𝐬^t\hat{\mathbf{s}}_{t} to the history.

C.2.3 Training

We employ a Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) approach to train both the Time2Decide model and the SFT baseline. Both models are initialized from a pretrained TimePFN checkpoint. The training objective is a combined loss function that jointly minimizes the error in return forecasting and portfolio allocation:

ℒ=λr​‖𝐫^−𝐫‖22+‖𝐬^−𝐬⋆‖22\mathcal{L}=\lambda_{r}\|\hat{\mathbf{r}}-\mathbf{r}\|_{2}^{2}+\|\hat{\mathbf{s}}-\mathbf{s}^{\star}\|_{2}^{2}

where 𝐫^\hat{\mathbf{r}} and 𝐫\mathbf{r} denote the predicted and ground truth return vectors, 𝐬^\hat{\mathbf{s}} and 𝐬⋆\mathbf{s}^{\star} denote the predicted and Oracle (optimal) allocation vectors, and λr\lambda_{r} is a hyperparameter that weights the return loss. We conduct a comprehensive hyperparameter sweep for λr∈{0,10,50,…,320000}\lambda_{r}\in\{0,10,50,\dots,320000\} to identify the optimal configuration for each model. Optimization is performed using the Adam optimizer with a maximum learning rate of 1×10−41\times 10^{-4} and a OneCycleLR scheduler with pct_start=0.3. The models are trained for a maximum of 50 epochs with a batch size of 32, employing early stopping with a patience of 5 epochs to prevent overfitting.

C.2.4 Evaluation Metrics

The metric for experimental evaluation is the Mean Squared Error (MSE) relative to the optimal Oracle strategy.

Crucially, to rigorously assess the models’ learning capability, we compute the MSE using the raw model predictions 𝐬~\tilde{\mathbf{s}} (before the feasibility projection described in the Inference section) against the Oracle allocations:

MSE=1T⋅Neval​∑n=1Neval∑t=1T‖𝐬~n,t−𝐬n,t⋆‖22\text{MSE}=\frac{1}{T\cdot N_{\text{eval}}}\sum_{n=1}^{N_{\text{eval}}}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\|\tilde{\mathbf{s}}_{n,t}-\mathbf{s}^{\star}_{n,t}\|_{2}^{2}

Appendix D Architectural Ablation: MLP, LSTM vs. Transformer

In our neural QP solver experiments, we include MLP and LSTM baselines designed specifically for QP inputs for comparison. The MLP is a deep residual network that flattens the input tokens into a single vector. It employs a 6-layer architecture with widths ranging from 6×6\times to 4×4\times the hidden dimension (d=256d=256), using pre-activation LayerNorm, ReLU, dropout, and projection-based residual connections to ensure trainability. The LSTM baseline processes the QP tokens sequentially using a 4-layer stacked LSTM with the same hidden dimension. Crucially, the LSTM shares the exact same input embedding and output MLP head as the transformer models, ensuring that performance differences arise solely from the sequence modeling mechanism (recurrence vs. attention). To ensure a fair comparison, the parameter counts of both baselines match those of our largest transformer model. In the following, we present the R2R^{2} results for the different models, where each problem dimension is evaluated using its best-performing transformer architecture.

Appendix E Additional Neural QP Solver Results

We present more results for neural QP solver experiments across higher problem dimensions beyond the main text’s focus on n=5,m=3n=5,m=3 configurations. See Tables 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, and 16 across problem sizes (n=7,m=3)(n=7,m=3), (n=7,m=6)(n=7,m=6), (n=10,m=3)(n=10,m=3), (n=10,m=6)(n=10,m=6), (n=10,m=9)(n=10,m=9), (n=15,m=10)(n=15,m=10), (n=20,m=8)(n=20,m=8), and (n=20,m=16)(n=20,m=16) respectively.

These comprehensive results demonstrate that transformers are capable of solving unseen QP problems of higher dimensions. Again, LinearTransformer consistently outperforms SoftmaxTransformer across problem dimensions and hyperparameter combinations. The entries marked as NaN indicate that the Transformer architecture with the specified depth ll and hidden dimension hh was unable to learn the QP solution for the given higher-dimensional problem and the data size, resulting in a negative R2R^{2}.

Additional Error Distributions.

Figures 4 through 9 present error distribution analyses for the best-performing configurations in higher-dimensional challenging QP problems (OPENn=10)n=10). These distributions complement performance metrics R2R^{2} by providing detailed information on the error characteristics of our transformer-based solvers. The figures show NMSE distributions, constraint violation patterns, and objective error distributions, revealing how both LinearTransformer and SoftmaxTransformer architectures handle the increased complexity of larger-scale QP instances.

Appendix F Toy Model: Statistical Suboptimality of Predict-then-Optimize

Problem Setup.

Consider two assets with random returns r1,r2r_{1},r_{2} having unknown means μ1,μ2\mu_{1},\mu_{2}. Let w∈[0,1]w\in[0,1] be the weight on asset 1. Define the mean gap δ:=μ1−μ2\delta:=\mu_{1}-\mu_{2}. For simplicity, we assume the assets are uncorrelated with equal variance. Consequently, the portfolio variance is proportional to w2+(1−w)2w^{2}+(1-w)^{2}, i.e.,

Var⁡(w​r1+(1−w)​r2)=σ2​(w2+(1−w)2).\mathrm{Var}\!\big(wr_{1}+(1-w)r_{2}\big)\;=\;\sigma^{2}\big(w^{2}+(1-w)^{2}\big).

Without loss of generality, we absorb the scale factor σ2\sigma^{2} into the risk-aversion parameter by redefining λ←λ​σ2\lambda\leftarrow\lambda\sigma^{2}; thus λ\lambda below should be interpreted as the coefficient on the variance term. We adopt a standard mean-variance utility:

U⁡(w,δ):=μ2+w​δ−λ⁡(w2+(1−w)2),λ>0.U(w;\delta)\;:=\;\mu_{2}+w\delta-\lambda\big(w^{2}+(1-w)^{2}\big),\quad\lambda>0.

By completing the square for the quadratic penalty, maximizing the utility is equivalent to minimizing the distance between ww and a shifted target. Letting u:=w−1/2u:=w-1/2, the objective simplifies to:

maxu∈[−1/2,1/2]uδ−2λu2.\max_{u\in[-1/2,1/2]}\quad u\delta-2\lambda u^{2}.

Because the toy-model utility is quadratic in ww with curvature 2​λ2\lambda, the utility suboptimality satisfies U⁡(w⋆,δ)−U⁡(w,δ)=2​λ​(w−w⋆)2U(w^{\star};\delta)-U(w;\delta)=2\lambda\,(w-w^{\star})^{2}, so MSE to the oracle allocation is directly proportional to the utility gap. This justifies MSE-to-oracle as the evaluation metric.

Assumptions.

This toy model makes several simplifying assumptions to enable closed-form insights. First, we consider only two assets with uncorrelated returns and equal variances, so the portfolio variance simplifies to σ2​(w2+(1−w)2)\sigma^{2}\!\left(w^{2}+(1-w)^{2}\right). Second, we use a mean–variance objective with fixed risk aversion λ>0\lambda>0 and a box constraint w∈[0,1]w\in[0,1], which induces the clipped linear decision rule. Third, we adopt a Bayesian formulation in which the true mean gap δ\delta follows a Gaussian prior 𝒩⁡(0,τ2)\mathcal{N}(0,\tau^{2}) and the estimate δ^\hat{\delta} is a noisy Gaussian signal; this conjugate structure yields the posterior mean 𝔼⁡[δ∣δ^]\mathbb{E}[\delta\mid\hat{\delta}] and the corresponding linear shrinkage factor in closed form.

Oracle vs. Predict-then-Optimize.

If the true gap δ\delta were known, the optimal allocation w⋆w^{\star} (derived by setting the derivative to zero and clipping to the feasible set) would be:

w⋆​(δ)=Π[0,1]​(12+δ4​λ).w^{\star}(\delta)\;=\;\Pi_{[0,1]}\left(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{\delta}{4\lambda}\right).

In the standard Predict-then-Optimize (PtO) approach, we observe samples, compute the empirical mean gap δ^=μ^1−μ^2\hat{\delta}=\hat{\mu}_{1}-\hat{\mu}_{2}, and simply plug it into the oracle formula:

wpto​(δ^)=Π[0,1]​(12+δ^4​λ).w_{\text{pto}}(\hat{\delta})\;=\;\Pi_{[0,1]}\left(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{\hat{\delta}}{4\lambda}\right).
End-to-End Learning. (E2E)

In contrast, an end-to-end learner seeks the action that maximizes expected utility given the noisy signal δ^\hat{\delta}. This corresponds to maximizing the conditional expectation:

𝔼⁡[U⁡(w,δ)∣δ^]=const+u​𝔼​[δ∣δ^]−2​λ​u2.\mathbb{E}[U(w;\delta)\mid\hat{\delta}]\;=\;\text{const}+u\,\mathbb{E}[\delta\mid\hat{\delta}]-2\lambda u^{2}.

The solution to this problem uses the posterior mean of the gap, not the raw estimate:

we2e​(δ^)=Π[0,1]​(12+𝔼⁡[δ|δ^]4​λ).w_{\text{e2e}}(\hat{\delta})\;=\;\Pi_{[0,1]}\left(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{\mathbb{E}[\delta|\hat{\delta}]}{4\lambda}\right).
The Gaussian Case: Explicit Shrinkage.

To see why the end-to-end policy outperforms PtO, assume a Gaussian prior on the true gap δ∼𝒩⁡(0,τ2)\delta\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\tau^{2}) and a sampling distribution δ^∼𝒩⁡(δ,s2)\hat{\delta}\sim\mathcal{N}(\delta,s^{2}) (where s2∝1/ns^{2}\propto 1/n). In particular, under the i.i.d. Gaussian return model with nn samples per asset, we have

s2=2​σ2n.s^{2}\;=\;\frac{2\sigma^{2}}{n}.

The posterior expectation is a linear shrinkage of the observed signal:

𝔼⁡[δ|δ^]=ρ​δ^,where ​ρ=τ2τ2+s2∈(0,1).\mathbb{E}[\delta|\hat{\delta}]=\rho\hat{\delta},\quad\text{where }\rho=\frac{\tau^{2}}{\tau^{2}+s^{2}}\in(0,1).

Substituting this into the general end-to-end update yields the explicit decision rule:

we2e​(δ^)=Π[0,1]​(12+ρ​δ^4​λ).w_{\text{e2e}}(\hat{\delta})\;=\;\Pi_{[0,1]}\left(\frac{1}{2}+\rho\frac{\hat{\delta}}{4\lambda}\right).

Comparing the equations for wptow_{\text{pto}} and we2ew_{\text{e2e}} reveals that PtO implicitly assumes ρ=1\rho=1. However, because ρ<1\rho<1 in finite samples, the end-to-end model outperforms PtO by shrinking the noisy estimate δ^\hat{\delta} toward the prior (zero), thereby reducing the variance of the decision. Moreover, since we2e​(δ^)w_{\text{e2e}}(\hat{\delta}) maximizes the conditional expected utility for each fixed δ^\hat{\delta}, for any measurable policy w⁡(δ^)∈[0,1]w(\hat{\delta})\in[0,1] we have

𝔼⁡[U⁡(we2e​(δ^),δ)|δ^]≥𝔼⁡[U⁡(w⁡(δ^),δ)|δ^].\mathbb{E}\!\left[U\!\left(w_{\text{e2e}}(\hat{\delta});\delta\right)\middle|\hat{\delta}\right]\;\geq\;\mathbb{E}\!\left[U\!\left(w(\hat{\delta});\delta\right)\middle|\hat{\delta}\right].

Taking expectations over δ^\hat{\delta} and using the tower property yields

𝔼⁡[U⁡(we2e​(δ^),δ)]≥𝔼⁡[U⁡(w⁡(δ^),δ)].\mathbb{E}\!\left[U\!\left(w_{\text{e2e}}(\hat{\delta});\delta\right)\right]\;\geq\;\mathbb{E}\!\left[U\!\left(w(\hat{\delta});\delta\right)\right].

In particular, choosing w​(δ^)=wpto​(δ^)w(\hat{\delta})=w_{\text{pto}}(\hat{\delta}) gives

𝔼⁡[U⁡(we2e​(δ^),δ)]≥𝔼⁡[U⁡(wpto​(δ^),δ)].\mathbb{E}\!\left[U\!\left(w_{\text{e2e}}(\hat{\delta});\delta\right)\right]\;\geq\;\mathbb{E}\!\left[U\!\left(w_{\text{pto}}(\hat{\delta});\delta\right)\right].
Empirical verification.

We empirically validate the conclusions of the toy model by Monte Carlo simulation. In each trial, we sample δ∼𝒩⁡(0,τ2)\delta\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\tau^{2}) and generate a noisy estimate δ^|δ∼𝒩⁡(δ,s2)\hat{\delta}\mid\delta\sim\mathcal{N}(\delta,s^{2}) with s2=2​σ2/ns^{2}=2\sigma^{2}/n. We then compute the PtO and end-to-end decisions

wpto​(δ^)=Π[0,1]​(12+δ^4​λ),we2e​(δ^)=Π[0,1]​(12+ρ​δ^4​λ),ρ=τ2τ2+s2,w_{\text{pto}}(\hat{\delta})=\Pi_{[0,1]}\!\left(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{\hat{\delta}}{4\lambda}\right),\qquad w_{\text{e2e}}(\hat{\delta})=\Pi_{[0,1]}\!\left(\frac{1}{2}+\rho\frac{\hat{\delta}}{4\lambda}\right),\qquad\rho=\frac{\tau^{2}}{\tau^{2}+s^{2}},

and evaluate the realized utility

U⁡(w,δ)=μ2+w​δ−λ⁡(w2+(1−w)2),U(w;\delta)=\mu_{2}+w\delta-\lambda\big(w^{2}+(1-w)^{2}\big),

averaging over 10510^{5} trials to estimate expected utilities. We also compute the oracle decision woracle​(δ)=Π[0,1]​(12+δ4​λ)w_{\text{oracle}}(\delta)=\Pi_{[0,1]}\!\left(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{\delta}{4\lambda}\right), which has access to the true δ\delta, and define regret as the expected utility loss relative to the oracle: Regret​(w)=𝔼⁡[U⁡(woracle)]−𝔼⁡[U⁡(w)]\text{Regret}(w)=\mathbb{E}[U(w_{\text{oracle}})]-\mathbb{E}[U(w)].

Results.

Figure 10 reports three key findings. Panel (a) shows the optimal shrinkage factor ρ\rho as a function of sample size nn; the shaded region represents the shrinkage effect that E2E exploits while PtO implicitly uses ρ=1\rho=1. Panel (b) compares the regret of both methods: E2E consistently achieves lower regret than PtO across all sample sizes, with the gap largest in the low-data regime and vanishing as n→∞n\to\infty (where ρ→1\rho\to 1). Panel (c) analyzes decision error |w−woracle||w-w_{\text{oracle}}| as a function of observed signal strength |δ^||\hat{\delta}|: PtO error grows linearly with |δ^||\hat{\delta}| because it overreacts to noisy estimates, while E2E error remains stable due to shrinkage. These results confirm the theoretical prediction that PtO is statistically suboptimal under finite-sample estimation noise, and that the suboptimality arises precisely from the failure to shrink predictions toward the prior mean.

Connection to Neural End-to-End Learning.

The closed-form rule

we2e​(δ^)=Π[0,1]​(12+ρ​δ^4​λ),ρ=τ2τ2+s2,w_{\text{e2e}}(\hat{\delta})=\Pi_{[0,1]}\!\left(\frac{1}{2}+\rho\,\frac{\hat{\delta}}{4\lambda}\right),\qquad\rho=\frac{\tau^{2}}{\tau^{2}+s^{2}},

shows that a decision-aware policy should shrink noisy estimates before optimizing, with the shrinkage level increasing as the effective estimation noise s2s^{2} grows. While the Bayes-optimal ρ\rho depends on unknown problem statistics (e.g., τ2\tau^{2} and s2s^{2}), an end-to-end trained model can implicitly learn an analogous attenuation from data by directly optimizing a downstream decision objective (e.g., expected utility/regret or supervision from oracle allocations). This viewpoint helps explain why Time2Decide can outperform PtO in practice: PtO effectively corresponds to ρ=1\rho=1, so it can overreact to noisy return signals, whereas Time2Decide can learn to temper its response when the signal-to-noise ratio is low. In particular, providing covariance information via our CAT tokenization supplies explicit second-order statistics about the market environment, which can inform how much to trust the return signal and yield more calibrated decisions under uncertainty.

Appendix G Negativity Case: Parity Barrier for Pure-Data Linear Attention

We show a simple obstruction: with only pure data tokens, linear attention cannot synthesize even-degree statistics (e.g., covariance). Intuitively, every attention layer contributes one factor of the data, so any finite stack remains an odd-degree function of the inputs unless we inject constants or explicit second-order tokens.

Proposition G.1.

Let tokens be zi=xi∈ℝnz_{i}=x_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} for i=1,…,Ni=1,\dots,N and let all per-token maps be linear: qj=xj​WQ,ki=xi​WK,vi=xi​WVq_{j}=x_{j}W_{Q},\ k_{i}=x_{i}W_{K},\ v_{i}=x_{i}W_{V}. With linear attention oj=∑i=1N⟨qj,ki⟩​vio_{j}=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\langle q_{j},k_{i}\rangle\,v_{i}, we have

oj=[∑i=1N(V​xi)​xi⊤]​M⊤​xj,M:=WQ​WK⊤,V:=WV,o_{j}=\Big[\sum_{i=1}^{N}(Vx_{i})x_{i}^{\top}\Big]M^{\top}x_{j},\qquad M:=W_{Q}W_{K}^{\top},\ \ V:=W_{V},

so ojo_{j} is linear in xjx_{j} and quadratic in {xi}i=1N\{x_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N}, hence an odd-degree function of the dataset. Consequently, such a layer and any finite stack cannot construct even-degree statistics like ∑i=1Nxi​xi⊤\sum_{i=1}^{N}x_{i}x_{i}^{\top} or any map invariant under the global flip xi↦−xix_{i}\mapsto-x_{i}.

Proof.

We compute

⟨qj,ki⟩=(xj​WQ)​(xi​WK)⊤=xj⊤​WQ​WK⊤​xi=xj⊤​M​xi.\langle q_{j},k_{i}\rangle=(x_{j}W_{Q})(x_{i}W_{K})^{\top}=x_{j}^{\top}W_{Q}W_{K}^{\top}x_{i}=x_{j}^{\top}Mx_{i}.

Thus

oj=∑i=1N(xj⊤​M​xi)​(V​xi)=(∑i=1N(V​xi)​xi⊤)​M⊤​xj=:SV​M⊤​xj,o_{j}=\sum_{i=1}^{N}(x_{j}^{\top}Mx_{i})\,(Vx_{i})=\Big(\sum_{i=1}^{N}(Vx_{i})x_{i}^{\top}\Big)M^{\top}x_{j}=:S_{V}\,M^{\top}x_{j},

where SV:=∑i=1N(V​xi)​xi⊤S_{V}:=\sum_{i=1}^{N}(Vx_{i})x_{i}^{\top} is a quadratic sketch of the data. Under the global sign flip xi↦−xix_{i}\mapsto-x_{i} for all i=1,…,Ni=1,\dots,N, we have SV↦SVS_{V}\mapsto S_{V}, while xj↦−xjx_{j}\mapsto-x_{j}, so oj=SV​M⊤​xj↦−ojo_{j}=S_{V}M^{\top}x_{j}\mapsto-o_{j}. Thus, the map is odd and cannot equal a flip-invariant even statistic such as ∑i=1Nxi​xi⊤\sum_{i=1}^{N}x_{i}x_{i}^{\top}. Each additional linear-attention layer multiplies by one more linear factor in the data, raising the degree by one, while linear/ReLU maps do not introduce even-degree terms. Therefore, no finite-depth stack of such components can yield even-degree statistics without adding constant channels or explicit second-order tokens. ∎

Empirical validation.

To validate this theoretical limitation, we conduct a simple covariance learning experiment where models must learn to estimate covariance matrices from unseen multivariate time series. We compare two transformer variants: (i) LinearTransformer with linear attention and input projection layers, and (ii) BasicLinearTransformer with linear attention and no input projection layers. Each model processes sequences of length 50 with 4 variables and predicts the empirical covariance matrix using the Frobenius norm loss. The models are trained on 5000 sample series and tested on 1000 sample series.

Tables 17 and 18 summarize the R² performance across different architectures and configurations. The results confirm our theoretical prediction: LinearTransformer achieves R² 0.9935, while BasicLinearTransformer (without input projection) performs significantly worse with R² 0.2827.

These empirical results support our theoretical analysis: while linear attention can learn covariance patterns when equipped with proper input projections/embeddings, removing these projections creates a fundamental barrier to learning even-degree statistics.
